title: A connected smooth affine group without nontrivial base-field tori is unipotent
statement: Let $k$ be an arbitrary field [def-weil-field]. All groups below are affine $k$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A torus is a group scheme whose extension to an algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure] is isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$ [def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type, def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $H$ be smooth and connected. Suppose every torus subgroup of $H$ defined over $k$ is the trivial subgroup. Then $H$ is unipotent: for some integer $n\geq1$ there is a closed immersion of $k$-group schemes $H\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_{n,k}\subseteq\mathrm{GL}_{n,k}$ [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-sc-general-linear-group], where $\mathcal U_{n,k}(A)$ consists of the upper triangular matrices over a commutative $k$-algebra $A$ with all diagonal entries equal to $1$. No perfectness, infinitude or characteristic assumption is imposed on $k$.

source.place: Proposition 17.81 and its proof, printed pp.378–379; Theorem 14.5, printed pp.281–282, for the unitriangular-immersion meaning of unipotence. The finite-field part of the proof invokes Proposition 17.99, printed pp.383–384.

proof.text: First suppose $k$ is infinite. Use strong induction on $d=\dim H$ to prove the assertion for every smooth connected affine torus-free $k$-group of dimension $d$. Apply [lem-sfb-infinitesimal-isogeny-lie-reduction] to $H$, obtaining $f:H\to G'$ with $\dim G'=d$. If $T'\subseteq G'$ is a torus, its lifting clause gives a torus $T\subseteq H$ with image $T'$; the hypothesis forces $T=1$, hence $T'=1$. Thus $G'$ is also torus-free. If $G'$ is unipotent, [lem-sfb-infinitesimal-isogeny-unipotence-reflection] proves the required unipotence of $H$. It remains to rule out nonunipotent $G'$ in the two cases of the reduction.

source.place: Proposition 17.81, printed p.379, infinite-field induction and isogeny case; Proposition 17.80, p.378.

proof.text: If $G'$ is nilpotent, apply [lem-sfb-nilpotent-central-torus-quotient] to obtain a central torus $T'$ with unipotent quotient $Q$. Since $G'$ is torus-free, $T'=1$, and the stated trivial-kernel clause identifies $G'$ with $Q$. Thus $G'$ is unipotent, contradicting the remaining case.

source.place: Proposition 17.81, p.379, nilpotent case; Theorem 16.47(a),(c), p.341.

proof.text: In the other case, $\operatorname{Lie}(G'_{\bar k})$ has a noncentral semisimple element. Since $k$ is infinite, [lem-sfb-infinite-field-semisimple-centralizer-reduction] supplies a smooth connected closed subgroup $K=C_{G'}(X)^\circ$ with $\dim K<d$ which is not unipotent. Every torus of $K$ is a torus of $G'$, hence trivial. The induction hypothesis applies to $K$ and says that it is unipotent, a contradiction. This also handles the base $d=0$: the second case would give a nonempty group $K$ of negative dimension, while the nilpotent case was settled without induction. Consequently the strong induction proves the infinite-field assertion.

source.place: Proposition 17.81, p.379, centralizer case, made precise with the identity component; Propositions 17.76–17.79, pp.377–378.

proof.text: Now suppose $k$ is finite. By [lem-sfb-finite-field-geometric-maximal-torus] choose $T\subseteq H$ with $T_{\bar k}$ geometrically maximal; the same statement ensures that $H_{\bar k}$ is smooth connected affine of finite type. The hypothesis makes $T=1$, so $T_{\bar k}=1$. Every torus $S\subseteq H_{\bar k}$ contains this trivial torus; maximality forces $S=1$. Apply [lem-sfb-no-torus-unipotent] over $\bar k$ to obtain a faithful closed representation $i:H_{\bar k}\to\operatorname{GL}_{a,\bar k}$ whose matrices $i(h)$ are unipotent for every $h\in H(\bar k)$.

source.place: Proposition 17.81, p.379, finite-field paragraph; Proposition 17.99, pp.383–384; Proposition 16.60, p.346.

proof.text: Choose a closed faithful representation $\rho:H\to\operatorname{GL}_{m,k}$ by [lem-sfb-affine-group-faithful-linear-representation]; its scalar extension is a rational representation of $H_{\bar k}$. For each $h\in H(\bar k)$, apply [lem-sfb-rational-representation-unipotent-point] with faithful representation $i$ from the preceding step and second representation $\rho_{\bar k}$. It gives $(\rho(h)-I_m)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$. Thus $\rho$ is injective on every algebra-valued point and all its geometric points are unipotent. Since $H$ is smooth affine of finite type, [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-unitriangular-embedding] applies over $k$ and gives the required closed immersion into $\mathcal U_{n,k}$ for some $n\geq1$. Together with the infinite-field case this proves the assertion over every field.

source.place: Corollaries 14.9 and 14.12, pp.282–283, and Theorem 14.5, pp.281–282; Theorem 4.9 and Corollary 4.10, p.87; paragraph 9.19, p.171.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 17.81, printed pp.378–379; the semisimple-centralizer case uses the connected identity component explicitly; Proposition 17.99, pp.383–384, supplies the finite-field case.
